newsitem.title: USA: Trade, tourism seen fueling Southeast in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Trade, tourism seen fueling Southeast in 1997.

text.p: Tourism, international trade and commercial construction will drive the Southeast economy to outperform the rest of the nation in 1997, bank economists predict.
Consumer spending is expected to slow below 1996 levels as credit card users become increasingly wary of adding debt.
But Charlotte, N.C.,-based First Union Corp. still projects GDP growth of 3.1 percent for the Southeast, compared with 2 percent nationally for 1997.
The Southeast's strongest gains will continue to come from Florida, Georgia, Tennesee and the Carolinas, First Union economist and Vice President Mark Vitner said.
Virginia and Maryland, harder hit by federal and military cuts, are gaining momentum but their performance will rise more in line with the rest of the country, he said.

Economists expect unemployment to remain low, with some sectors experiencing labour shortages. Already in Florida, corporate growth has been stalled by a dearth of entry-level service workers and highly skilled computer programmers.

"We are looking at a situation where employers are having to pay a bounty to fill some positions," said Lynn Reaser, chief economist for Barnett Banks Inc., based in Jacksonville, Fla., "There will be some upward pressure on wages but it will mainly involve particular skill types."
Exports of Southeast manufactured goods, which rose more than 6 percent in 1996 to a record $75 billion, should rise slightly faster in 1997, Vitner said.
The strongest gains have been in the Carolinas, Virginia and Florida, with the biggest impact in the port communities of Miami and Tampa, Fla.; Charleston, S.C.; Savannah, Ga.; and Hampton Roads, Va.
"Miami in particular will be the major beneficiary in improvements in Latin America, with growth of trade in that whole region," Reaser said.

The region's shipyards are also experiencing a renaissance, due to renewed riverboat construction, Navy contracts and expanding need for commercial cargo ships, the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta said.
Tourism will remain strong, especially among visitors from Latin America, Canada and Europe, Reaser predicted.

The visitor boon will keep Orlando, Fla.; Nashville, Tenn.; and Myrtle Beach, S.C.; at the top of the metropolitan growth list, Vitner predicted. All are seeing major investment in new and bigger tourism and convention facilities, especially Orlando, where Walt Disney Co. and Universal Studios are building major expansions.
Banking is doing well throughout the region, while health care and financial services continue to fuel Alabama's economy, especially in Birmingham, Vitner said.
Perhaps the biggest influence on the South's economy this year will come from commercial construction, which has already risen more than 75 perent during the 1990s, Vitner said.

In Georgia, the frenzy of Olympic construction forced delays in planned commercial projects. Florida also is racing to catch up with "significant backlogs" in non-residential projects, especially warehouses and retail space, Reaser said.

However, Vitner said, "We're nowhere near seeing overbuilding in commercial real estate. The only market that may see some problem is apartments, but even there the levels of construction that we've had in the 1990s are far below what we saw in the 1980s."
The bloodletting is over in the Southeast's textile and apparel manufacturing, which has been the biggest drag on the region's economy.
"I would expect layoffs to stop and to see some small job gains in the textiles and apparel," Vitner said.
